title: The trap question
hook: Prince Abhaya brings a two-horned question; the answer depends on truth, benefit and timing

segments.voice: Yesterday: kukkura, Seniya's dog vow, and deeds that bear fruit like themselves. Your line: you become the habit.

Have you stopped wasting your money? Yes or no. Either answer sinks you. The sutta calls this kind of question two-horned: whichever way you answer, a horn catches you. Prince Abhaya is handed one by a rival teacher and sent to try it on the Buddha. It will stick in the Buddha's throat like an iron hook, the teacher promises: he can neither swallow it nor spit it out. Make him answer, and people will say Abhaya refuted the great Gotama.
screen: `HAVE YOU STOPPED WASTING MONEY?` → `A TWO-HORNED QUESTION.` → `PRINCE ABHAYA TRIES IT.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Prince Abhaya. The question: would the Buddha ever say something unwelcome, something that hurts another person? If yes, how is he different from an ordinary person who hurts people? If no, why did he say of his cousin Devadatta that he was headed for ruin, which made Devadatta furious? Abhaya asks. And the Buddha says: there's no one-sided answer to that. Abhaya admits the plan has already failed, and confesses the whole plot. Now, Abhaya happens to have a baby boy on his lap. So the Buddha asks: if this child, while you weren't looking, put a stick or a pebble in his mouth, what would you do? I'd take it out, Abhaya says. If I couldn't get it right away, I'd hold his head with one hand and hook it out with a finger of the other, even if it drew blood. Why? Out of compassion for the child. Just so, the Buddha says. Then he lays out how he speaks. If something is untrue, or true but not beneficial, he doesn't say it, welcome or not. If it is true and beneficial, he knows the right time to say it, welcome or unwelcome. Three questions: is it true? Is it beneficial? Is this the time? Sometimes a true, helpful word stings, like a finger in a baby's mouth, and he says it anyway, out of compassion. The trap had two horns. The Buddha answered with three questions.
screen: `WOULD YOU EVER SAY WHAT HURTS?` · `NO ONE-SIDED ANSWER` · `A PEBBLE IN A BABY'S MOUTH` · `TRUE? BENEFICIAL? THE RIGHT TIME?` · then, large: `TRUTH, BENEFIT, TIMING.`

segments.voice: Think of something you need to say that feels tricky, a hard truth for a friend, an honest answer at work, and run the three questions slowly: is it true, is it helpful, is now the time? If all three are yes, picture saying it, plainly and kindly; if not, let it wait. Then rest in the breath.
Abhaya. The prince who brought a two-horned riddle, answered with a baby, a pebble, and three tests for speech.
Your line: truth, benefit, timing. Kindness sometimes means a hard word at the right time. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists study MN 58 as a guide to right speech: say only what is true and beneficial, and choose the right time, whether or not it is welcome; some teachers summarize it as checking truth, benefit and timing before speaking.

myth: the Buddha never says anything unwelcome
if something is true and beneficial, he says it at the right time, welcome or not.
the Buddha used the baby on Abhaya's lap to answer
a father would hook a pebble from his child's mouth even if it drew blood, out of compassion.
anything true should be said at once
true but not beneficial isn't said; true and beneficial waits for the right time.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a prince asks: would you ever say something that hurts someone? yes seems to make you ordinary; no seems to contradict what you told Devadatta. what do you say?
options: there's no one-sided answer to that.
fork.reveal: the Buddha refuses both horns, then uses the baby on Abhaya's lap to show that truth, benefit and timing decide what he says.

trapdoor: what you thought: kind speech means only saying nice things.
what it means: kind speech is true, beneficial and well-timed, even when it stings.
what a scholar hears: MN 58 sorts speech into six cases by true or untrue, beneficial or not, welcome or not; the Buddha speaks only in the two that are true and beneficial, at the proper time.
guess: the prince who brought the Buddha a trap
a rival teacher who wanted to win a debate
the Buddha's cousin, who grew furious

chat.says: Is it ever kind to tell someone something that hurts?
options: Yes, if it's true, helpful and timely: like hooking a pebble from a baby's mouth.
Never; the Buddha said kind people only say what others want to hear.
Always; any true thing should be said right away, whatever the cost.
chat.meaning: In MN 58 the Buddha speaks true, beneficial words, even unwelcome ones, at the right time, out of compassion, like taking a pebble from a child's mouth.

Abhaya.meaning: a prince sent to trap the Buddha with a question

two-horned.meaning: a question that catches you whichever way you answer

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (the discourse to Prince Abhaya)

notes: MN 58 paraphrased: Nigantha Nataputta gives Abhaya the two-horned question (the 'rival teacher' is not named in the script to keep the focus on the speech teaching), the Devadatta reference, the child on his lap, the six cases of speech. Confirm.
The opening example ('have you stopped wasting your money?') is the script's modern illustration, not from the text.
